newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa chief sees European price war.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa chief sees European price war.

text.p: The leader of German airline Lufthansa AG said on Tuesday he expected a major fare war similar to that seen in the United States in the 1980s when Europe's skies are fully liberalised on April 1.

Lufthansa management board chairman Juergen Weber told the Hamburg Abendblatt newspaper in an interview that a new wave of upstart airlines will take on existing airlines just as some 150 new airlines emerged in the U.S. after deregulation.
"The major European airlines will presumably not take on one another in their home markets," Weber said in the interview. "That would be too expensive."

But Weber, predicting Lufthansa would survive, said small airlines would seek to break into selected markets by offering sharply lower prices, making the situation in Germany more competitive and driving domestic airfares "into the cellar".

"A number of people seeking adventure are going to turn up in the German market," Weber said, noting Lufthansa earns 56 percent of its profits on European routes and that Europe would be a major "battlefield" in the coming years.

Weber said he expected the price war to cause stagnant sales growth or losses in Germany, while the European market would likely show growth of below five percent. Intercontinental routes would likely show sales growth of 5-10 percent, he said.

Weber reiterated that Lufthansa would seek to strengthen its presence in Asian markets, where it sees the largest chance for growth, and that Lufthansa was "intensively negotiating" with some Asian airlines to set up more cooperation deals.
"Japan and China are among the most interesting markets. I will not say anything more," Weber said.

Lufthansa currently operates about 70 to 80 aircraft in Germany and carries annually about 11 million passengers, with Weber predicting the current downturn of airfares in Germany of about two to five percent accelerating in the coming months.
He specifically saw the most danger from airlines such as Britain's Virgin Express and Easy Jet and other competitors with operating costs up to 20 to 30 percent below Lufthansa.

Lufthansa has been under severe pressure in Germany from rival Deutsche BA, which is 49 percent owned by British Airways Plc, and also from the German cartel office which ruled in February that Lufthansa was overcharging on flights between Berlin and Frankfurt where it faces no competition.

Lufthansa has said it may pull out of the Frankfurt-Berlin route and instead use its Condor charter unit to operate flights. Rival Eurowings has said it would team up with Air France to fly the route with fares up to 50 percent cheaper.

Weber said Lufthansa would keep up cost-cutting efforts aimed at reducing operating costs by 1.5 billion marks by the year 2000 but declined to rule out that Lufthansa may set up units to operate some of its European routes with cheaper workers.
"We want to work with existing Lufthansa workers but we must remain competitive," Weber said. "If we do not, then there are two alternatives -- lose the business or use workers from another company."

Weber said the high level of subsidies for European airlines would delay a wave of bankruptcies, as was seen in the United States shortly after deregulation and saw major airlines such as Pan Am and Eastern disappear from the skies.

But Weber said consumers in the end may be hurt by the deregulation move since many airlines will not survive the fight and may lead to a small group of major airlines controlling routes and demanding higher fares than before.
He also dismissed speculation that Lufthansa would build up its franchise network of regional airlines that operate code-share flights for Lufthansa.
Lufthansa will annually invest about one to two billion marks in new aircraft in the coming years and increase its fleet to 345 aircraft from the current level of 312, he said.
